UNITED PRESS


WASHINGTON, May 16.—Warning that the federal government must face immediately the facts of unemployment relief on scale greater than proposed by President Herbert Hoover, and by means of direct federal aid rather than loans to the states, was uttered in the senate today by Senator William Borah rep. Idaho.


"It is war," Borah shouted. "It is a contest to preserve government, and the moral and physical well-being of the citizenship."


Borah read to the senate the warning served upon Mr. Hoover by the railway brotherhoods that they would not assume responsibility for orderly operation of the lines, nor for disorder that was bound to develop unless something were done.


Far from being agitators, Borah said, those are men of thought and character.

CHOOLS open tomorrow. The


public schools, the junior high


schools. the high schools and the
- majority Of private and parochial


educational institutions in WASH
tngton end the Summer vacation Mon
day. flinging open wide their doors to
what is estimated $4,000 children.


Many youthful ones Will be making
their pilgrimages for the first time.
But. regardless of the number OF prior
visits countless numbers of boys and
girls between the hours of and 9
O'Clock will be on their individual ways.
Thoughts of old friendS-What the new
teacher is going to be like-and what
seats they will occupy will be in their
minds At the same time motorists
will be on their way through the city
and it is up to these motorists to be
most careful.


A Plea by Van Duzer.


William A. Van Duzer, through the
Traffic Department, of which he Is the
director, has issued pleas for safe and
sane driving. particularly in the neigh
borhood of schools. Accidents Of Sc
rious nature and fatalities among the
school children Of Washington have
been comparatively low. Mr.. Van Duzer
wants this record maintained and I'M
proved. II want every driver to drive
carefully at all times" Mr.. Van Duzer
states. But want every driver to
drive with more than the usual amount
Of care near the schools. Slow down at
all times when children are grouped
around. Come to complete stop. II
doing so removes all chances Of an
accident. Many children do not realize
the perils of traffic. They are young and
thoughtless. But any one old enough
to drive car is old enough to be thor
oughly acquainted with the necessity
Of being cautious


New signs last week bearing the word
''school" have been painted on the streets
near the schools. Crosswalks also are
being indicated in these sections Those
not finished by tomorrow will be by the
end of this week. The American Auto
mobile Association, with the co-opera-
ton of the Police Department, again

By the Associated Press.


URBANA, Ill., December 3.—Promise of improved prices for corn is seen by DR. L. J. Norton, specialist on the history and trend of farm prices at the University of Illinois.


There is nothing in the history of corn prices or in the general economic situation, he says, to suggest that the farm price of corn will remain at "absurdly low" prices now current.


Already, DR. Norton declares, there is promise of higher prices from forces now being set in motion to use up the crop.


In the Northeast States, for instance there has been an active commercial movement," he explains. Some export trade has developed. Recently there has been a small direct movement of corn from the Illinois Valley to California by all-water route."


Cites Storage Space.


Farmers themselves, in DR. Norton's opinion, believe corn prices soon are due to rise. As evidence he points to extensive emergency corn-storage space being used this year in corn States.


Contrary to some reports, he says, this year's corn crop of more than 6,864,000,000 bushels is not the largest on record, although corn is the cheapest of 20 leading farm products on the basis of prevailing index prices.


In spite of an increased acreage of nearly 10 per cent since 1928," DR. Norton explains, "the country has harvested larger corn crop than is reported for 1882 in three of the last 15 years.


The increase in production is largely concentrated in West States, but around edges of the belt—in South Dakota, Kansas, PENNSYLVANIA, Kentucky and Lee the crop is lighter.


Movement Retarded.


High transportation costs tend to retard the movement from the surplus areas to these deficit districts. This reduces prices in surplus areas."


Among other encouraging factors, he notes that more cattle are being fed and steps being taken to expand a somewhat reduced hog output.


Corn also is being used as fuel to a limited extent, and all these things, taken together, help use up the crop and bolster prices."
